title: Myers v. United States (1926)
summary: The Court invalidated a statutory requirement that the Senate consent to removal of a presidentially appointed postmaster.
notes: Chief Justice Taft wrote for a 6-3 Court affirming the Court of Claims' rejection of the salary claim; Justices Holmes, McReynolds and Brandeis each dissented. Myers was the first-class postmaster at Portland, Oregon, removed by Wilson in 1920, and the suit was brought by his administratrix.

sections.Parties: Myers challenged his removal as a first-class postmaster by President Wilson; the United States defended presidential removal authority. The excerpt’s editorial introduction identifies the 1920 removal and the relevant 1876 statute.
sections.Material Facts: The Postal Services Appropriations Act required presidential appointment and removal of first-, second-, and third-class postmasters with Senate advice and consent, with four-year terms unless lawfully removed sooner. Wilson discharged Myers without Senate consent. The dispute therefore involved an additional congressional role in removing an officer appointed by the President and Senate.
sections.Procedural History: The Supreme Court adjudicated the constitutional validity of the removal restriction and held it invalid.
sections.Issue: Did the Constitution permit Congress to require Senate consent before the President removed this executive officer?
sections.Holding: No. The Court held that the statutory denial of unrestricted presidential removal authority over first-class postmasters violated the Constitution.
sections.Reasoning: Taft linked removal to the President’s constitutional responsibility for faithful execution and the ability to supervise executive officers. He read the congressional debates of 1789 as recognition of a constitutionally grounded removal power. The opinion distinguished limits on directing a particular quasi-judicial decision from the ability to remove an official after evaluating performance. It also recognized prior authority permitting Congress to regulate removal of inferior officers whose appointment it vested in department heads, and expressly left some questions unresolved. Holmes emphasized Congress’s authority to create, abolish, and define the tenure of statutory offices; the editors summarize similar concerns in the omitted McReynolds and Brandeis dissents. Humphrey’s Executor later confines Myers’s binding reach and rejects broader language inconsistent with its own ruling.

topics.lrs-s-removal: The Court associated presidential supervision and faithful execution with power to remove this executive officer.
topics.lrs-s-congressional-control: The statute required Senate participation in removal, a feature later decisions distinguish from simple for-cause protection.
topics.lrs-s-agency-independence: Myers's broad removal holding is the baseline that Humphrey's Executor narrowed to permit independent agencies.
